passage: When I was seven, I was sure the tall thin glass had more juice. My cousin Salma poured the same juice into a short fat bowl, and I shouted, "Now there's less!" She just laughed, said, "Watch, Sachin," and poured it back into the tall glass. It came up to the same line. I stared. I made her do it three times. Now I'm ten, and last week my little brother cried because his clay snake was "bigger" than his clay ball. I squashed the snake back into a ball, the same size as before. He didn't believe me either. I remember how that felt.

qa.q: Where did Salma pour the juice from the tall glass?
qa.a: Into a short fat bowl.

qa.q: Why did young Sachin make Salma pour it three times?
qa.a: Sachin was surprised and unsure, and wanted to check with his own eyes that the amount really stayed the same.

qa.q: How could Sachin help the little brother understand?
qa.a: Let him roll and squash the clay himself many times, so he sees it for himself rather than being told.

qa.q: How does Sachin see the little brother's confusion now?
qa.a: Sachin understands it, remembering believing the same thing at seven.

grounding: It shows a child looking back on learning that an amount stays the same when its shape or container changes.

passage: Maths corner note, Gargi, Class 3 teacher. We tested water today with a tall bottle and a wide tray. I poured one cup into each. Most children said the bottle had more because the water stood higher. Kunal, eight, frowned and said, "No, it's the same cup. You didn't add any." When Ravi said the tray looked like more, Kunal said, "It's just spread out, like a chapati is flat but it's the same dough." I asked him to prove it; he poured the tray back into the cup, and it filled to the brim. Next week I will try the same test with clay.

qa.q: Which two containers were used?
qa.a: A tall bottle and a wide tray.

qa.q: What does Kunal's frown suggest before he answered?
qa.a: He seemed puzzled that others thought the amount had changed, since he was sure nothing had been added.

qa.q: Why was asking Kunal to prove it a good step?
qa.a: It turned his idea into something the whole class could see, not just a claim.

qa.q: How might Ravi see Kunal's chapati example?
qa.a: It may help him understand, because it uses something he knows from home.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a child reasoning that the amount of water is unchanged by the container's shape.

passage:
Diary, Sunday night.
Played shop with my little brother Vishal. I gave him ten coins in a tight pile and kept ten for me in a long line. He cried, "You have more!" I said, "Count." He counted mine: ten. He counted his: ten. He still said mine was more because it was longer. So I spread his out even longer than mine. He grinned. "Now I have more!" I laughed so much. Last year I think I'd have believed that too. Now it's obvious to me that spreading coins doesn't make more of them. Tomorrow I'll try the water trick on him. 😄
- Tushar

qa.q: How many coins did each child have?
qa.a: Ten coins each.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when Vishal said "Now I have more!"?
qa.a: Tushar was amused and laughed a lot, and it was also a reminder of how much Tushar's own thinking had changed since last year.

qa.q: What could Tushar try so that Vishal really understands?
qa.a: Line the coins up in pairs, one of his next to one of Vishal's, so Vishal can see none are left over.

qa.q: Why does Vishal believe the longer line is more?
qa.a: He is judging by how long the row looks rather than by the number, which is common for younger children.

grounding: It shows a child who now understands that the number of coins stays the same however they are spread out.

passage: In their village kitchen, Manjula Ajji poured buttermilk from a tall steel glass into a wide brass bowl for Arohi. 'Ajji, you gave me less!' Arohi said, pointing at how low it sat. Ajji smiled. 'Did I pour any out?' Arohi frowned. 'No...' 'Then pour it back.' Arohi carefully tipped it into the glass. It came right up to the same mark. She stared. 'It's the same! The bowl is just fat.' She drank it straight from the bowl, giggling.

qa.q: What did Ajji pour the buttermilk into?
qa.a: She poured it from a tall steel glass into a wide brass bowl.

qa.q: Why did Arohi stare when the buttermilk reached the same mark?
qa.a: She was surprised to discover the amount hadn't changed, only the shape of the container.

qa.q: What made Ajji's approach effective?
qa.a: She asked a question and let Arohi test it herself, so Arohi reached the answer on her own.

qa.q: How might Manjula Ajji have felt watching Arohi pour the buttermilk back?
qa.a: Ajji probably enjoyed it, since she smiled and let Arohi discover for herself that the amount had not changed.

grounding: Illustrates a child understanding that a quantity stays the same when its container changes shape, in a village.

passage: On a hot afternoon in Nairobi, Jamal and Emeka each got a carton of mango juice. Jamal poured his into a tall, thin glass. Emeka poured his into a short, wide cup. 'Mine's more!' Jamal said. Emeka rolled his eyes. 'Same carton, same juice.' 'But mine's higher.' Emeka took both cartons and showed him: empty, same size. Then he poured his cup into another tall glass. Level with Jamal's. Jamal looked from one to the other. 'Okay. Same. But mine still looks better.'

qa.q: Who poured juice into the short, wide cup?
qa.a: Emeka poured his juice into the short, wide cup.

qa.q: How was Jamal feeling when he said 'But mine still looks better'?
qa.a: He had accepted they were the same, but he felt a little embarrassed and wanted to save face with a joke.

qa.q: What did Emeka's demonstration show, and why did it work?
qa.a: Pouring into a matching tall glass showed the same level, which proved the amount didn't change, only the container's shape.

qa.q: What would change if Jamal were much younger?
qa.a: He might keep insisting the tall glass had more, because younger children often judge by height alone.

grounding: Shows a child grasping that liquid quantity is conserved when poured into containers of different shapes, in Kenya.

passage: In the Class 2 science room, Gautam, the teacher, poured water from a tall thin glass into a wide bowl. "More, less or the same?" he asked. Most children shouted, "Less!" Pradeep, seven, frowned. "Same. You didn't add any or take any out." "But it looks lower," said his partner. Pradeep took the bowl and poured it back into the glass. "See? Back to the same line." Gautam smiled. "Pradeep, explain again for everyone."

qa.q: What did Gautam pour the water into?
qa.a: A wide bowl.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep frown when the others shouted "Less!"?
qa.a: He was puzzled because he felt sure it was the same amount and disagreed with the class.

qa.q: What did Gautam do well, and what could come next?
qa.a: He let Pradeep prove it by pouring back; next he could try the same idea with rice or clay.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's partner feel when the water reached the same line?
qa.a: Surprised, and perhaps curious about why it looked like less.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that the amount of water stays the same when poured into a different-shaped container.

passage: I'm Trisha, Tejas's big sister. Last Sunday he was making clay animals. I rolled one ball into a long snake. "Now yours has less," I teased. Tejas, who's seven, looked at it, then said, "No. You just made it long." "Look, mine's bigger!" "It's the same clay, Didi. Roll it back." I did. It was the same ball. He crossed his arms and grinned. Last year he'd have cried that I had more. I can't know how he worked it out, but he was very sure.

qa.q: What did Trisha roll the clay ball into?
qa.a: A long snake.

qa.q: What does Tejas crossing his arms and grinning suggest?
qa.a: He felt confident and pleased that he was right about the clay.

qa.q: How could Trisha keep building on Tejas's understanding?
qa.a: Try other changes with him, like flattening or breaking the clay, and ask if the amount changes.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Tejas's change since last year?
qa.a: She notices he used to cry about having less but now understands the clay stays the same.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that clay keeps the same amount when its shape changes, seen by an older sister.

passage: Monday: Sahil, seven, poured his mango juice into a tall glass and his little brother Ojas's into a short cup. "I have more!" he said. Their mother poured both into two identical glasses: the same. Sahil stared. Wednesday: Sahil poured his juice into a bowl on purpose, then back into his glass. "Same," he muttered. Friday: Ojas cried that his juice in a wide cup was less than Sahil's in the tall glass. Sahil sighed like a teacher. "It's the same juice, it's just a fatter cup."

qa.q: What did Sahil pour into a bowl on Wednesday?
qa.a: His juice.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he stared at the identical glasses on Monday?
qa.a: He was surprised and confused, since he had been sure he had more.

qa.q: What helped Sahil understand over the week?
qa.a: Testing it himself by pouring the juice back and forth.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel when Sahil explains it's the same juice?
qa.a: Maybe still unsure, since at his age it looks like less, but reassured by his brother.

grounding: Shows a child coming to understand across a week that juice stays the same amount in different containers.

passage: Ganga Nani pulled Jagdish closer. "When I was seven, my mother poured milk for me and my brother, Shyam. Mine was in a tall, thin steel glass. His was in a wide bowl. I cried, 'Mine is more!' and Shyam shouted, 'Mine is more!' Our uncle came in, laughed and poured my glass into another bowl just like Shyam's. The milk came up to exactly the same place. I stared at it for a long time. That night I kept pouring water between cups in the kitchen, tall to short to tall, checking. Your great-uncle still teases me about it." Jagdish grinned. "I would've wanted the bowl."

qa.q: What kind of glass was Ganga's milk in?
qa.a: A tall, thin steel glass.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel as she stared at the milk in the two bowls?
qa.a: She was puzzled and surprised that the milk came up to exactly the same place.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what could Ganga's uncle have done if she still wasn't sure?
qa.a: The turning point was the uncle pouring the milk into a matching bowl; he could have let her pour it back and forth herself.

qa.q: How might young Shyam have seen the argument?
qa.a: Shyam likely felt equally sure his bowl had more, since both children judged by shape.

grounding: A grandmother recalls learning that milk stays the same amount when poured from a tall glass into a bowl.

passage: The school bus was due in five minutes, and there was one bottle of mango juice. Sumit poured half into a tall plastic cup and half into a short wide one. Madhav, his younger cousin, grabbed the tall one. "Mine's bigger!" "It's the same," Sumit said, racing for his shoes. "No, it's taller!" The horn honked outside. Sumit took the tall cup, poured it into a short one like his, and set them side by side. "See? Same line." Madhav stared, then drank fast. "Okay, same." They ran for the bus, juice moustaches on both.

qa.q: How long until the school bus was due?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he grabbed the tall cup?
qa.a: He felt pleased and sure he had more juice because the cup was taller.

qa.q: How did Sumit show Madhav the amounts were equal?
qa.a: He poured the juice from the tall cup into a matching short cup to show the same line.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt about having to explain it in a hurry?
qa.a: He was probably stressed about missing the bus, but determined to be fair.

grounding: Rushing for the bus, an older boy shows a younger cousin that juice stays the same when poured into a different cup.

passage: In art class at the Chennai school, Karthik rolled his clay ball into a long snake. Pankaj pointed. "Now you have way more clay than me!" Karthik looked at his snake, then at Pankaj's round ball. "No, I don't. I didn't add anything. I just made it long." "But it's longer." "Watch." Karthik rolled the snake back into a ball, the same size as Pankaj's. "Same." Pankaj squinted. "Then do it again." Karthik laughed and rolled it out. "It's still the same, whatever shape."

qa.q: What did Karthik roll his clay ball into?
qa.a: A long snake.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he saw the snake?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit envious, believing Karthik had more clay.

qa.q: How did Karthik show the amount of clay was the same?
qa.a: He rolled the snake back into a ball the same size as Pankaj's.

qa.q: What would change if Karthik had only argued without rolling it back?
qa.a: Pankaj might stay unconvinced, since seeing the ball return to its size made the point clear.

grounding: A boy in art class shows a friend that clay stays the same amount whatever its shape.

passage:
"No fair! You got more juice!" Disha said, pointing at Chaitanya's tall, thin glass.

"No, I didn't. Mummy poured the same."

"Yours goes up higher."

"Because it's thinner. Watch." Chaitanya poured his juice into a jug. Then he poured Disha's into another jug the same size. "See? Same level."

Disha squinted. "Oh."

"The glass changes shape, not the juice."

"Then I want the tall glass. It looks like more."

Chaitanya laughed. "It's still the same, silly."

qa.q: What kind of glass did Chaitanya have?
qa.a: He had a tall, thin glass.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when she thought Chaitanya had more?
qa.a: Disha felt it was unfair and a bit jealous.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya show that the amount was the same?
qa.a: He poured both juices into same-size jugs to show the same level.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the argument about the glasses?
qa.a: Mummy might be amused, since she poured the same amount and the quarrel is only about the shape of the glasses.

grounding: A child shows another child that the amount of juice stays the same even when the glass changes shape.

passage:
During Diwali holidays, Dolma and I made clay diyas at her house. I was eight.

I rolled a ball of clay, and Dolma flattened hers into a pancake. "Mine's bigger," she said.

I was sure she was right. It looked huge.

Her grandmother came in. "Roll it back," she said. Dolma rolled it into a ball, and it was the same size as mine.

I remember staring at it. The clay hadn't changed. Only the shape. I'm Kishore, and even now, every Diwali, I think of that pancake.

qa.q: What did Dolma flatten her clay into?
qa.a: She flattened hers into a pancake.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel staring at the rolled-back clay?
qa.a: Kishore felt amazed and surprised, realising the amount hadn't changed.

qa.q: How did Dolma's grandmother help the children learn?
qa.a: She asked them to roll it back so they could see for themselves.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel when her clay turned out the same size?
qa.a: Dolma might feel surprised and a bit disappointed that hers wasn't bigger.

grounding: A child looks back on a Diwali when clay changing shape showed the amount stays the same.

passage:
Science note, winter term.

Noor, nine, filled a short, wide bowl with water and froze it overnight. The next day she let it melt and poured it into a tall, narrow glass.

Her friends said, "There's more now!" Noor said, "No, it's the same water. It just looks taller."

To prove it, she poured it back into the bowl. It filled to the same line.

I asked her to show the class tomorrow. — Dhruv

qa.q: What did Noor pour the melted water into?
qa.a: She poured it into a tall, narrow glass.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when her friends said there was more?
qa.a: Noor was likely confident and a little amused, sure it was the same water.

qa.q: How did Dhruv support Noor's understanding?
qa.a: Dhruv asked Noor to show the class, letting her explain her reasoning.

qa.q: How might her friends feel after she poured it back?
qa.a: Her friends were probably surprised and convinced.

grounding: A teacher notes a child showing that a quantity of water stays the same when its container changes shape.

passage:
Dear Diary, 2 May, summer holidays
It was so hot today that Mummy made mango panna. She poured one full steel tumbler for me and one for Sunaina. Then Sunaina tipped hers into the tall thin glass and shouted, "Now I have more!" Mummy laughed and asked me. I looked hard. The tall glass looked fuller, but I poured it back into the tumbler and it filled it exactly, not a drop more. "Same amount, it just changed shape," I said. Sunaina sulked and said I was cheating. Tomorrow I'll show her with water and the measuring jug.
Gargi

qa.q: What did Mummy make because it was so hot?
qa.a: She made mango panna.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after pouring the panna back into the tumbler?
qa.a: Gargi felt sure and satisfied, having proved that the amount stayed the same. 😊

qa.q: How could Gargi help Sunaina see the idea tomorrow?
qa.a: Gargi could let Sunaina do the pouring with water and the measuring jug, so Sunaina sees the level match.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina think the tall glass has more?
qa.a: Sunaina judges by how high the drink reaches, so the tall thin glass looks fuller, and being told otherwise feels like cheating.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that the amount of a drink stays the same when it is poured into a differently shaped glass.
